title: lexical-seeding-heuristics-notebook
content:
Lexical seeding heuristics — quick log

Context / motivation
- Trying to build a compact set of practical heuristics for when to "seed" lexical cues in prompts vs. when to rely on structural framing and examples.
- Lexical seeding = intentionally inserting short, high-salience tokens/phrases early in the prompt (or examples) that bias decoder toward desired register/format/semantics. Useful for tiny templates where token budget is constrained.
- This doc is a scratchpad: experiments, micro-patterns, failure cases, and short recipes to try in the Prompt Library.

High-level heuristics (working)
1) Use explicit lexical anchors when you need consistent surface form. Example: want answers that always start with a single-digit code or a bracketed tag ("[OK]"). Anchors reduce variance.
2) Prefer structural cues (delimiters, example pairs) for semantic constraints; lexical seeding is brittle to paraphrase.
3) Avoid seeding culturally/ideologically loaded tokens — they amplify priors and cause asymmetric errors across demographics.
4) If model is repeating the seed too literally across examples, add paraphrase variance in the exemplars (one exact anchor, others softened).
5) For retrieval-style tasks, seed with domain-specific jargon to improve relevance (but watch OOV tokenization effects).

Micro-experiments (notes and results)
- Experiment A: bracket-anchor for classification
  Prompt A1: "Classify the sentiment. Answer as ONE WORD in brackets: [POSITIVE] or [NEGATIVE]"
  Result: high compliance with bracket rule but model sometimes spells bracket tokens out when punctuation is trimmed.
  Lessons: keep anchor token contiguous and isolated on its own line if you control whitespace.

- Experiment B: tokenized seed vs. phrase seed
  Setup: seed with single token 'ALPHA' vs phrase 'use alpha-style tag' in 3-shot few-shot set.
  Observations: single-token seeds are more robust across temperature and are less paraphrased by model; phrase seeds sometimes lead model to reinterpret as instruction rather than tag.

- Experiment C: morphological perturbation test (tokenization boundary)
  Idea: test 're:budget' vs 're budget' vs 'rebudget' as seeds.
  Result: certain compound forms are split into tokens that reduce prompt salience on smaller models; for quantized LMs (int8) the predictor seems to latch on to whole-token anchors more reliably.

Few-shot recipes (3 examples unless noted)
A) Compact QA style with lexical signal - Seed line: "Tag: TRI"
Ex1: Q: "Where to park?" A: "Tag: TRI — Surface lot near gate B."
Ex2: Q: "How long is the warranty?" A: "Tag: TRI — 12 months, parts only."
Ex3: Q: "Are batteries included?" A: "Tag: TRI — No."
Prompt for inference: provide question + "Tag:" line and expect concise answer after the tag.
Notes: works well for short outputs; fails when question needs explanation >2 sentences.

B) Few-shot with paraphrase variance to reduce lexical overfit
Example set intentionally rewrites anchor wording across examples so the model learns the intent rather than exact string.
Pattern: one example uses exact anchor 'ALPHA', second uses 'alpha tag:', third uses 'label:alpha'.

Failure modes observed (examples)
- Over-literalization: model repeats anchor verbatim across outputs, even when context conflicts (e.g., anchor said "Always use X" but input says "Don't use X").
- False-positives: lexical seeding can cause the model to hallucinate presence/attributes just because the seed token is correlated in the few-shot set.
- Fragility to punctuation stripping: systems that normalize punctuation or remove brackets (downstream token sanitizer) break the anchor heuristics.
- Demographic bias amplification: seeding with region-specific names or terms increases skew in entity resolution tasks.

Quantitative checks to run for any candidate seed pattern
- Compliance rate: % outputs containing seed or target format.
- Precision @1 of label vs ground truth (for classification).
- Diversity penalty: measure n-gram overlap between exemplar outputs and model outputs to detect parroting.
- Breakpoint T-test: test performance with and without tokenization perturbations (space added/removed) to quantify brittleness.

Quick checklist for adding a seeded template to Prompt Library
- [ ] Does the application require exact surface form? If no, prefer structural framing.
- [ ] Run tokenization boundary check on smallest supported model.
- [ ] Add 1–2 paraphrase variants in exemplars.
- [ ] Smoke test with punctuation stripping and lowercase-only input.
- [ ] Run demographic skew quick-audit if seed contains names/locations.

Mini-examples (failure reproduction steps)
1) Repro script: take 50 dev prompts, inject seed 'TAGX' at start, record output tokens, compute rate of hallucinated attributes for inputs that explicitly contradict the anchor.
2) Paraphrase test: generate 20 paraphrases per exemplar using the model, then rerun few-shot classification to see shift in label distribution.

Unresolved questions / open ideas
- Can we learn a minimal set of lexical seeds per domain via a tiny search (beam search over 2–3 token candidates) instead of hand-picking? Need budgeted search experiment.
- Interaction with quantization: anecdotal hint that int8/int4 runtimes change anchor salience. Should include runtime-tagged benchmarks (hosted vs dedicated).
- Is there a reliable way to convert lexical seeds into structural constraints via post-processing (e.g., map any output containing synonyms to canonical tag)? Could help mitigate over-literalization.

Next steps (short term)
- Implement small benchmarking harness: 200 examples x 10 seed variants x 3 models (tiny, base, large) — measure compliance, precision, and parrot-overlap. Owner: Priya (me).
- Add results as a new PR to prompt-lab repo and create a one-pager for PD.

Random notes to self
- Avoid the word 'anchor' in public docs until we have clear mitigation guidance (sounds too prescriptive).
- Talk to SRE about whether whitespace normalization is happening on ingestion path (LIN ticket).
- Share initial failure cases in next Prompt Lab sync (Wed).

References and quick links
- PR: github.com/redwood-inference/prompt-lab/pull/412 (seeded-template harness)
- Linear: LIN-789 (tokenization boundary failures)
- Slack thread: #prompt-lab oddities (see linked URL above)

End of scratch log. Save as working draft — prune later and move canonical heuristics to prompt-library/heuristics/ when stable.
